title: Cisco CCNP Wireless Study Guide
description: CCNP Wireless is Cisco's newest professional track — launched March 19, 2026, when all wireless content was carved out of CCNP Enterprise into a dedicated certification: the new WLCOR core plus a design (WLSD) or implementation (WLSI) concentration. If you're a wireless engineer who was studying ENWLSD/ENWLSI under the old structure, the transition rules matter and this guide covers them.
audience: Wireless-focused network engineers — WLAN designers, Wi-Fi implementation specialists, and campus engineers whose real work is RF, roaming, and controllers rather than routing tables. Also the landing spot for engineers displaced by ENCOR v1.2's wireless removal: this track is where that career lane now lives.
why_get_it: Because as of March 2026, this is the ONLY Cisco professional path for wireless careers — ENCOR v1.2 dropped all wireless content, and the old Enterprise wireless concentrations (ENWLSD/ENWLSI) tested for the last time on March 18, 2026. The new track brings the curriculum current: WLCOR covers wireless core technologies including the Wi-Fi 6/7 era, and the concentrations carry the renamed, realigned design and implementation exams. Every exam passed earns a Specialist credential, and WLCOR doubles as the qualifying exam for the renamed CCIE Wireless. Being early to a new track cuts both ways: the credential is maximally current, and the study ecosystem is minimal — mostly official sources for now.
when_to_get_it: If wireless is your lane, now is genuinely a strategic moment: transition credit rules honor recent ENWLSD/ENWLSI passes (within 3 years) as WLSD/WLSI equivalents — meaning engineers holding one of those exams can complete CCNP Wireless by passing WLCOR alone. Check your CertMetrics status before planning. Fresh candidates need CCNA-level fundamentals plus real WLAN exposure; this is a professional-tier exam set, and wireless depth (RF behavior, roaming, controller architecture) can't be crammed from theory.
salary_note: No track-specific salary data exists yet for a certification this new — anchor to the role: senior WLAN and wireless network engineers typically post $95–135K in U.S. markets, with large-venue, healthcare, and warehouse-automation wireless (the genuinely hard RF environments) at the top. Directional and third-party; specialist scarcity in wireless has historically paid a modest premium over generalist campus roles.
exam_format: Two proctored exams at Pearson VUE (test center or OnVUE): the WLCOR v1.0 core plus one concentration (WLSD design or WLSI implementation, both v1.2 — the renamed ENWLSD/ENWLSI). Counts and passing scores not published.

recertification_note: 3-year cycle, 80 CE credits on the unified ledger — WLCOR re-pass = 80 CE, a concentration = 40. Standard professional-tier rules from day one of the new track.

study_steps.title: Check your transition credit before anything else
study_steps.description: If you passed ENWLSD (300-425) or ENWLSI (300-430) within the last 3 years, that pass counts as WLSD/WLSI credit — you may be one WLCOR exam away from the full CCNP Wireless. Verify your status in CertMetrics; this is the cheapest professional cert completion available to anyone it applies to.

study_steps.title: Study from official sources — the ecosystem is newborn
study_steps.description: A track launched in March 2026 has almost no third-party material yet: the WLCOR blueprint on CLN, Cisco U's official paths, and Cisco Live wireless sessions carry the load. Old ENWLSD/ENWLSI materials remain useful for the concentrations (they're renames), but WLCOR v1.0 is genuinely new — budget accordingly.

study_steps.title: Respect the RF floor
study_steps.description: Wireless is the one networking discipline where physics grades your work. If RF fundamentals are shaky — propagation, interference, channel planning — front-load them; every WLCOR domain assumes them. The CWNP vendor-neutral materials remain the community's favorite RF foundation even for Cisco tracks.

study_steps.title: Lab with what wireless allows
study_steps.description: Wireless labbing is inherently physical, but the controller side virtualizes: Cisco's DevNet sandboxes cover Catalyst wireless controllers and Meraki APIs, and dCloud runs guided wireless demos. For RF practice, a couple of used APs and a survey app teach more than any simulator.

study_steps.title: Pick the lane by your deliverable
study_steps.description: WLSD if your value is surveys, designs, and the documents that precede deployment. WLSI if it's controllers, cutover nights, and the airtime problems after. Shops usually need both skills; the exam choice just declares your lead foot.

study_steps.title: Sit WLCOR, then the concentration
study_steps.description: $400 + $300, standard professional format, no lab exam. Passing WLCOR also qualifies you for the renamed CCIE Wireless (whose practical went v1.1 with Wi-Fi 6/7 and Meraki content) if the expert tier calls later.

study_steps.title: Position for the moment
study_steps.description: Wi-Fi 7 refresh cycles, high-density venue buildouts, and warehouse automation are driving real wireless demand — and this brand-new credential is maximally current for all of it. Being early can read as currency in the shops that track Cisco's catalog — anecdotal, not measured, but the credential itself is verifiably the most current wireless cert Cisco has ever shipped.

faq.question: What happened to wireless in CCNP Enterprise?
faq.answer: It moved out entirely. ENCOR v1.2 (March 19, 2026) removed all wireless topics, and the Enterprise wireless concentrations ENWLSD/ENWLSI tested for the last time on March 18, 2026. Wireless careers now certify here: CCNP Wireless, with the new WLCOR core and the renamed WLSD/WLSI concentrations. One era's concentration became the next era's track.

faq.question: I passed ENWLSD or ENWLSI — do I get credit?
faq.answer: Yes, if it's recent: passes within the last 3 years count as the equivalent WLSD/WLSI credit, meaning WLCOR alone completes your CCNP Wireless. Verify in CertMetrics and plan around it — this transition window is the cheapest professional-cert completion Cisco has offered in years.

faq.question: Is it too early to pursue a track this new?
faq.answer: Depends on your tolerance for thin study ecosystems. The credential itself is maximally current (Wi-Fi 6/7 era content) and being early can read as currency in Cisco-tracking shops (anecdotal, not measured) — but third-party courses and question banks barely exist yet, so you'll lean on official sources, CWNP fundamentals, and real experience. Wireless veterans: fine time. Wireless newcomers: build the RF foundation first regardless.

faq.question: What about CCIE Wireless?
faq.answer: It was renamed too — CCIE Enterprise Wireless became CCIE Wireless in March 2026 — its qualifying exam changed from ENCOR to WLCOR (first testable March 19, 2026), and its practical went v1.1 with Wi-Fi 6/7 and Meraki content. Your WLCOR pass qualifies you. Same expert-tier economics as every CCIE: $1,600 per 8-hour lab attempt.

faq.question: CCNP Wireless or CWNP's ladder?
faq.answer: Different bets, honestly both respectable: CWNP (CWNA→CWDP/CWAP→CWNE) is vendor-neutral, physics-first, and beloved by RF purists; CCNP Wireless is Cisco-stack-specific and reads louder in Cisco-standardized enterprises. The classic answer stands — CWNA-level RF knowledge underneath, vendor cert on top — and nothing about the new track changes it.
